formation.title: The Sengoku Ends
formation.text:
The last embers of the Sengoku Jidai have been extinguished. Across the provinces of Japan, the banners of rival clans no longer fly in defiance. They have been torn down, burned, or pledged anew to the victorious house. The emperor sits in Kyoto as he always has, but real power now flows from one source alone.

The unifier faces a choice that will shape generations. The methods of conquest (massed ashigaru, castle sieges, the ruthless subjugation of rivals) can be turned outward, building Japan into a military power that dominates East Asia. Or the sword can be sheathed, the energies of the nation redirected toward internal development, peace, and the prosperity that comes from two centuries without war. Or perhaps the moment calls for something higher: the elevation of Japanese civilization itself, a cultural flowering that makes the islands the envy of the known world.

Which path shall define the new Japan?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Tenka Fubu: the realm under one sword.

modifiers.name: Tenka Fubu
modifiers.text: The realm under one sword. From the ashes of the Sengoku Jidai rises a Japan united by military supremacy, where the strongest clan has imposed order through force of arms and the mastery of combined infantry and firearms tactics.

options.text: Seek the Pax Tokugawa: prosperity through peace.

modifiers.name: Pax Tokugawa
modifiers.text: The long peace. With the warring states subdued, Japan turns inward to cultivate its domains. Rice paddies expand, castle towns flourish, and the merchant class grows prosperous under the stable order of centralized rule.

options.text: We are the Land of the Rising Sun. Let our culture shine.

modifiers.name: Land of the Rising Sun
modifiers.text: A civilization apart. United Japan asserts its unique cultural identity: the perfection of the tea ceremony, the refinement of bushido, and the flowering of arts that will define Japanese civilization for centuries.

advances.name: Za Merchant Guilds
advances.text: The establishment of za, monopolistic merchant guilds operating under the patronage of temples, shrines, and noble houses during the Muromachi era.

advances.name: Tachi Forging
advances.text: The art of forging the tachi: the long curved sword of the mounted samurai, predecessor to the katana and symbol of the warrior class.

advances.name: Shoen Estates
advances.text: The system of private estates held by aristocrats, temples, and warrior houses that forms the economic foundation of medieval Japan.

advances.name: Shugo Administration
advances.text: The appointment of military governors, shugo, to administer provinces on behalf of the shogunate, establishing a framework for centralized control.

advances.name: Wokou Traditions
advances.text: The maritime raiding traditions of the wokou pirates who terrorized the coasts of Korea and China, forging Japan's earliest naval capabilities.

advances.name: Nanbokucho Legacy
advances.text: The enduring legacy of the Northern and Southern Courts period: a divided era that nonetheless established the legitimacy of imperial succession and the political structures that would shape Japan.

advances.name: Muromachi Culture
advances.text: The flourishing of Zen-influenced arts under the Ashikaga shoguns: ink painting, Noh theater, the tea ceremony, and the dry landscape gardens that define Japanese aesthetics.

advances.name: Yari Ashigaru
advances.text: The organization of peasant foot soldiers into disciplined formations armed with long yari spears, transforming warfare from individual samurai combat to mass infantry tactics.

advances.name: Za Expansion
advances.text: The growth of merchant guilds beyond their temple patrons, developing independent monopolistic control over production, transport, and sale of key commodities.

advances.name: Yamashiro Fortification
advances.text: The construction of mountain fortresses, yamashiro, that exploit Japan's rugged terrain to create nearly impregnable defensive positions.

advances.name: Tally Trade
advances.text: The system of regulated maritime trade with Ming China using official tally certificates, establishing Japan's position in the East Asian trading network.

advances.name: Sohei Traditions
advances.text: The warrior monk tradition of the great Buddhist monasteries, fearsome fighters who wield the naginata in defense of their temples and the faith.

advances.name: Tanegashima Firearms
advances.text: The adoption of Portuguese matchlock rifles, tanegashima, and their rapid mass production by Japanese smiths, forever changing the nature of Japanese warfare.

advances.name: Nanban Trade
advances.text: Trade with the 'southern barbarians': Portuguese and Spanish merchants who bring firearms, Christianity, and exotic goods to Japan's shores.

advances.name: Castle Revolution
advances.text: The transformation from mountain fortresses to lowland castles with massive stone walls, wide moats, and towering keeps: the architectural signature of the Sengoku era.

advances.name: Hayabune Patrol Fleet
advances.text: Fast coastal patrol vessels that guard Japan's extensive coastline against pirates, smugglers, and foreign intruders.

advances.name: Ikko-Ikki Suppression
advances.text: The systematic crushing of the militant Ikko-ikki Buddhist uprisings, ending the era of religiously motivated peasant rebellions and consolidating secular authority.

advances.name: Daiku Tradition
advances.text: The master carpenter tradition, daiku, whose skills in joinery, castle construction, and temple building represent some of the finest woodworking in the world.

advances.name: Tamahagane Smithing
advances.text: The art of smelting iron sand in the tatara furnace to produce tamahagane: the jewel steel from which Japanese blades are forged.

advances.name: The Sword Hunt
advances.text: The katanagari: the systematic confiscation of weapons from the peasantry to consolidate the samurai monopoly on violence.

event.title: The Great Sword Hunt
event.text:
In the aftermath of unification, an edict is proclaimed across every province: all swords, short swords, bows, and firearms in the hands of the common people are to be confiscated. The official reason given is that the metal will be melted down to forge nails and bolts for a great statue of the Buddha: a pious fiction that few believe but all obey.

The true purpose is unmistakable. By disarming the peasantry, the new order draws an uncrossable line between the warrior class and everyone else. Never again will farmers take up arms in ikki uprisings or rally behind ambitious local lords. The sword hunt transforms Japan's social order as profoundly as any battle, establishing a monopoly on violence that will endure for centuries.

options.text: Let the swords be gathered.

modifiers.name: Katanagari Decree
modifiers.text: The great sword hunt has stripped the peasantry of their weapons, consolidating the instruments of violence in the hands of the samurai class alone. Order is restored, and rebellion grows far less likely.

advances.name: Kenchi Land Survey
advances.text: Comprehensive cadastral surveys that measure every rice paddy and field, establishing a rational basis for taxation and domain administration.

advances.name: Tekkōsen Ironclads
advances.text: Massive oar-driven warships sheathed in iron plate, the floating fortresses that dominate Japanese coastal waters.

advances.name: Korean Campaigns
advances.text: The large-scale military expeditions to the Korean peninsula, ambitious campaigns that tested Japan's unified military might against continental powers.

advances.name: Christian Expulsion
advances.text: The systematic persecution and expulsion of Christian missionaries and converts, asserting Japanese religious sovereignty and eliminating a perceived threat to social order.

advances.name: Sankin-Kotai
advances.text: The system of alternate attendance, requiring daimyo to maintain residences in Edo and travel there regularly, draining their treasuries while enriching the capital.

event.title: Sankin-Kotai Proclaimed
event.text:
A masterful instrument of control has been devised: the system of alternate attendance. Every daimyo in Japan must now maintain residences in both Edo and their home domain, traveling between them on a fixed schedule. Their wives and children remain in Edo permanently, honored guests who happen to be hostages.

The financial burden is staggering. The processions of each daimyo (hundreds or thousands of retainers, all in full ceremonial dress) must travel the great roads at enormous expense. Lodgings, gifts, and the maintenance of grand Edo mansions drain domain treasuries. What gold might have been spent on armies and fortifications instead flows into roads, inns, and the coffers of Edo merchants.

It is, perhaps, the most elegant system of political control ever devised. The daimyo are kept loyal not by the threat of force, but by the steady hemorrhage of their wealth.

options.text: A system worthy of admiration.

advances.name: Controlled Trade
advances.text: The restriction of foreign trade to designated ports under strict government supervision, maintaining sovereignty while preserving access to essential goods.

event.title: Sakoku: The Closed Country
event.text:
The edicts have been proclaimed: Japan shall close its doors to the world. Portuguese missionaries are expelled. Spanish traders are banned. The English factory at Hirado is shuttered. Only the Dutch and Chinese are permitted to trade, and only at the tiny artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki harbor, under the strictest supervision.

Japanese subjects are forbidden from traveling abroad on pain of death. Those already overseas may never return. The great ocean-going ships are ordered destroyed, replaced by coastal vessels too small to cross open water.

Yet the closure is not absolute. Through Dejima, a trickle of Western knowledge continues to flow, books on medicine, astronomy, and military science that a small circle of scholars study as rangaku, Dutch learning. The question is whether Japan will use this isolation to perfect its own civilization, or whether it will fall behind the Western powers that even now are exploring the globe.

options.text: Seal the borders: our civilization needs no outside influence.

modifiers.name: Sakoku Consolidation
modifiers.text: With foreign influence carefully controlled, Japan turns inward. The stability of isolation allows domestic institutions to mature without outside disruption.

options.text: Maintain the Dutch window. Knowledge knows no borders.

modifiers.name: Rangaku Window
modifiers.text: Through the tiny window of Dejima, Dutch learning seeps into Japan. Medical texts, astronomical charts, and natural philosophy filter through the handful of interpreters who speak the language of the red-haired barbarians.

advances.name: Hatamoto Guard
advances.text: The direct retainers of the shogun, elite warriors who form the professional core of the Tokugawa military establishment.

advances.name: Genroku Culture
advances.text: The golden age of Edo-period arts: kabuki theater, haiku poetry, ukiyo-e woodblock prints, and the refined aesthetics of the tea ceremony.

event.title: The Genroku Renaissance
event.text:
Under the long peace, Japanese culture has reached unprecedented heights. In Edo, Osaka, and Kyoto, the merchant class patronizes arts that would have been unimaginable during the chaos of the Sengoku. Kabuki theater draws packed audiences, the haiku reaches its perfection in the verses of the wandering poets, and woodblock prints capture the floating world of pleasure quarters and natural beauty.

The tea ceremony has evolved from a simple ritual into an elaborate philosophy of aesthetics. Ceramic arts produce wares sought by collectors across East Asia. The puppet theater of bunraku achieves a dramatic sophistication that rivals any stage in the world. Even the martial arts, freed from the urgency of actual warfare, are refined into formalized schools of swordsmanship and archery.

This is the paradox of the Tokugawa peace: a warrior society that, forbidden from fighting, channels its energies into creating one of the most refined civilizations in human history.

options.text: Let a thousand flowers bloom.

advances.name: Temple Schools
advances.text: Terakoya, community schools run by Buddhist temples and retired samurai that teach reading, writing, and arithmetic to commoner children.

advances.name: Machi Bugyou
advances.text: The town magistrate system, efficient urban administrators who maintain order, settle disputes, and manage the bustling commercial life of Japan's great cities.

advances.name: Rangaku Studies
advances.text: The systematic study of Western science and technology through Dutch texts, laying the intellectual groundwork for Japan's future modernization.

event.title: Rangaku: Dutch Learning
event.text:
For generations, a small cadre of scholars in Nagasaki has pored over Dutch texts, laboriously translating works on anatomy, astronomy, botany, and military science. What began as idle curiosity has grown into a serious intellectual movement.

The breakthrough came with the translation of a Dutch anatomy text, when Japanese physicians discovered that their traditional Chinese medical charts were riddled with errors, while the Western diagrams matched what they actually observed in dissections. The implications were profound: the barbarians, for all their crude manners, possessed genuine knowledge that Japan lacked.

Now rangaku schools proliferate across the country. Domain lords sponsor scholars to study Western gunnery and fortification. Physicians adopt Western surgical techniques. Astronomers correct centuries of accumulated error. A quiet revolution in knowledge is underway: one that will prepare Japan for the shock of forced opening that lies ahead.

options.text: Knowledge is the greatest weapon.

advances.name: Kaibogaku Defense
advances.text: Coastal defense studies combining traditional fortification with Western military science, preparing Japan against the threat of foreign naval power.

advances.name: Han Reforms
advances.text: Administrative modernization of the domain system, rationalized taxation, bureaucratic efficiency, and fiscal reform led by progressive daimyo.

advances.name: Proto-Industrialization
advances.text: The emergence of cottage industries, sake breweries, and textile workshops that begin to transform Japan's economy from pure agriculture toward manufacturing.

advances.name: Fukoku Kyohei
advances.text: Enrich the country, strengthen the military: the rallying cry of Japan's modernizers who seek to build a nation capable of standing among the great powers.

event.title: Fukoku Kyohei
event.text:
Enrich the country, strengthen the military: the slogan echoes across Japan as a new era dawns. The old order is crumbling, whether from internal pressure or the threat of foreign gunboats matters less than the response. Japan must transform itself or be consumed.

Two visions compete. The first looks to the Chrysanthemum Throne: the emperor, sidelined for centuries by the shogunate, can serve as the unifying symbol of a centralized modern state. Imperial restoration would concentrate authority, sweep away the fragmented domain system, and channel national energies under a single sovereign will.

The second vision looks westward. What Japan needs is not merely new leadership but new knowledge: the sciences, industries, and institutions that have made the Western powers dominant. Send students abroad. Hire foreign advisors. Build railroads and telegraph lines. The nation that modernizes fastest survives.

Perhaps both paths lead to the same destination. But the emphasis chosen now will shape Japan's character for generations.

options.text: Restore the Emperor: Sonno Joi!

modifiers.name: Imperial Restoration
modifiers.text: The emperor has been restored as the true sovereign of Japan. Legitimacy flows once more from the Chrysanthemum Throne, and the centralized state draws strength from this ancient source of authority.

options.text: Seek civilization and enlightenment: Bunmei Kaika!

modifiers.name: Bunmei Kaika
modifiers.text: Civilization and enlightenment! Japan casts aside the old constraints and embraces wholesale modernization, Western science, industry, and institutions are adopted with breathtaking speed.

advances.name: Meiji Precursors
advances.text: The intellectual and political movements that foreshadow the Meiji Restoration, calls for imperial rule, Western learning, and the transformation of Japan into a centralized modern state.

destiny.name: The Destiny of Japan
destiny.text: Japan stands unified for the first time in generations. The garrisons are strengthened, the domains consolidated. Now the question is: what will this new Japan become?

event.title: The Destiny of Japan
event.text:
The last rival banners have fallen. Japan is one. But unity is not a destination; it is a beginning. The question that now confronts the ruling house is as old as civilization itself: what does a great nation do with its power?

The answer will define not merely Japan's future, but its very character. Shall the sword that united the islands be turned outward, carving an empire from the coasts of Asia? Or shall it be sheathed, its energies channeled into building a civilization so refined and prosperous that conquest becomes unnecessary?

options.text: Our destiny awaits.

destiny.name: Northern Pacification
destiny.text: Secure the wild northern frontier of Ezo, from the Ishikari plain to Shizunai, where Shakushain raised the Ainu against the Matsumae in 1669. Control of these territories establishes the northern boundary of the Japanese empire. Requires owning Ishikari and Shizunai with a substantial army.

conditions.text: Own Ishikari, or a subject owns it
Own Shizunai, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Northern Frontier Secured
event.text:
The wild lands of Ezo have been brought under Japanese authority. The Ainu peoples, who once roamed these northern territories unchallenged, now answer to Japanese administrators. From the Ishikari plain to Shizunai, where Shakushain once raised the river chiefs against the Matsumae, the banner of the unified state flies.

These conquests are more than territorial additions. Ezo's forests, fisheries, and potential farmland represent a vast new resource base, and its northern shore looks toward Karafuto and the continent beyond.

The military machine that conquered these territories is now tested, hardened, and hungry for greater challenges. The continent beckons.

options.text: The frontier is secure. What lies beyond?

destiny.name: Korean Expedition
destiny.text: Launch a full-scale invasion of the Korean peninsula, seizing the capital at Hanseong and the southern port of Gyeongju. Japan's armies must prove they can fight and win on continental soil. Requires the conquest of Korea, and the age of the Kenchi land survey, by whose assessed yields each domain owes its men.

conditions.text: Own Namgyeong, or a subject owns it
Own Gyeongju, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Rising Sun Over Korea
event.text:
Japanese armies have crossed the strait and planted their banners on continental soil. Hanseong, the Korean capital, is in Japanese hands. Gyeongju, seat of ancient Silla glory, acknowledges Japanese supremacy. The invasion that many thought impossible has succeeded.

But holding conquered territory differs from taking it. Two approaches present themselves. The first favors raw military power, maintaining a permanent samurai vanguard on the peninsula, ready to crush any resistance and push further into Manchuria. The second takes a subtler approach, establishing a tributary system that preserves local governance while extracting tribute and obedience.

One demands more blood. The other demands more patience.

options.text: Station our samurai as a permanent vanguard.

modifiers.name: Samurai Vanguard
modifiers.text: A permanent garrison of elite samurai stationed on the Korean peninsula, ready to crush resistance and push deeper into the continent. The cost in war-weariness is real, but so is the military capability.

options.text: Establish a tributary system of vassal states.

modifiers.name: Tributary System
modifiers.text: A network of vassals and tributaries that acknowledges Japanese supremacy while preserving local governance. Tribute flows to Japan; obedience follows. New wars are easier to justify through this established order.

destiny.name: Greater Asian Sphere
destiny.text: Japan's military ambitions reach their apex. From the Philippines to Taiwan, the islands of the Pacific and the coasts of Asia fall under Japanese hegemony. This is the culmination of Tenka Fubu on a continental scale. Requires Tondo, Formosa and a massive army.

conditions.text: Own Tondo, or a subject owns it
Own Basai, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Greater Asian Sphere
event.text:
From Formosa to the Philippines, from Korea to the southern seas, the Japanese sphere of influence encompasses a vast arc of Asian territory. What began with the unification of the home islands has grown into something no Japanese ruler ever imagined: a maritime empire to rival those of the European powers.

Two visions for this empire compete. The naval faction argues that Japan's destiny lies on the waves: a Pacific dominion connected by sea lanes, defended by fleets, and enriched by trade. The continental faction counters that true power lies in territory: that Japan must secure its position on the Asian mainland through overwhelming military strength.

The choice will determine whether Japan becomes a thalassocracy or a land empire.

options.text: Our destiny lies on the Pacific waves.

modifiers.name: Pacific Dominion
modifiers.text: Japan commands the Pacific through naval supremacy. The Imperial fleet dominates the sea lanes from Taiwan to the Philippines, though maintaining such a vast maritime force draws resources from the army.

options.text: True power is measured in land held.

modifiers.name: Continental Hegemon
modifiers.text: Japan's armies are the dominant land force in East Asia. Fortresses and supply lines support operations deep into the continent, though the navy suffers from the diversion of resources to the army.

destiny.name: Domain Economy
destiny.text: The wealth of a united Japan flows through its silk markets and gold reserves. Consolidate the domain economy into a coherent trading system that enriches the central authority. Requires substantial gold reserves, high stability, and silk in the market.

conditions.text: A market the country is in

children.text: Silk is produced in the market
Silk is traded in the market

event.title: The Domain Economy Flourishes
event.text:
The economic reorganization of Japan is bearing fruit. The domain lords, once petty warlords who funded their ambitions through rice taxes alone, now preside over diversified local economies. Silk flows from Nishijin looms, gold fills the coffers of Edo money-changers, and the great roads connecting castle towns hum with merchant traffic.

The central authority, drawing revenue from this growing commercial web, finds itself wealthier than any shogunate in history. Trade centers in Osaka, Sakai, and Hakata process goods from across the realm. Banking houses extend credit that lubricates the wheels of commerce.

Japan's economy, once fragmented among hundreds of quarreling domains, has become a coherent national system. The long peace is paying dividends.

options.text: Prosperity is the truest measure of good governance.

destiny.name: The Floating World
destiny.text: Under the long peace, Japan's cities swell with merchants, artisans, and artists. The ukiyo (the floating world of pleasure quarters, kabuki theaters, and woodblock prints) becomes the envy of civilizations. Requires castle towns in three places, the seeds of the great cities, national prestige and gold reserves.

conditions.text: A Jokamachi stands in at least 3 of our locations

event.title: The Floating World
event.text:
The long peace has wrought a transformation that no general could have achieved. Japan's cities (Edo, Osaka, Kyoto) are among the largest and most sophisticated in the world. In the pleasure quarters and theater districts, a vibrant urban culture has emerged that the warriors of the Sengoku would not recognize.

Two aspects of this cultural flowering compete for patronage. The merchant houses of Osaka and Sakai have grown fabulously wealthy, their trading networks extending across East Asia. They fund kabuki theater, sponsor artists, and quietly accumulate the real power that comes from controlling the flow of money.

Meanwhile, the artists and poets of the ukiyo, the floating world, create works of breathtaking beauty. Woodblock prints, haiku poetry, and kabuki performances define a civilization at its cultural peak.

Which aspect shall the state encourage?

options.text: Empower the merchant houses of Osaka.

modifiers.name: Merchant Houses of Osaka
modifiers.text: The great merchant houses control the flow of money and goods across Japan. Their wealth funds espionage networks and commercial ventures, though the influx of capital brings inflationary pressure.

options.text: Patronize the arts of the floating world.

modifiers.name: Ukiyo Culture
modifiers.text: The floating world of art, theater, and poetry reaches its zenith. Japan's cultural prestige endures, and its refined reputation improves diplomatic relations. The mercenary arts, however, are beneath such a cultured nation.

destiny.name: Eastern Workshop
destiny.text: Japan transforms from an agrarian society into an industrial power. Factories, shipyards, and zaibatsu conglomerates drive modernization at breathtaking speed. Requires Shiranuka on Hokkaido's coal coast, gold reserves, and coal in the market.

conditions.text: Own Shiranuka, or a subject owns it
A market the country is in

children.text: Coal is produced in the market
Coal is traded in the market

event.title: The Eastern Workshop
event.text:
Japan has achieved what seemed impossible: an industrial revolution on its own terms. The coal mines of Hokkaido feed blast furnaces. Shipyards launch modern vessels. Railways connect cities that were once weeks apart. The zaibatsu, great industrial-financial conglomerates, have become the engines of national transformation.

Two models of industrial development present themselves. The zaibatsu-led approach concentrates economic power in a handful of great firms (Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Sumitomo) that combine banking, trade, and manufacturing under single corporate umbrellas. They are ruthlessly efficient but create dangerous concentrations of private power.

The alternative is the kokusan policy: national production directed by the state, building strategic industries under government control to ensure that Japan's modernization serves the national interest rather than private profit.

options.text: Let the zaibatsu lead Japan's modernization.

modifiers.name: Zaibatsu Power
modifiers.text: Industrial-financial conglomerates drive Japan's modernization with ruthless efficiency. Their global reach extends Japan's commercial range, and their wealth attracts mercenary talent, though rapid expansion strains supply lines.

options.text: National production for the national interest.

modifiers.name: Kokusan Policy
modifiers.text: State-directed national production ensures that Japan's industrial capacity serves the national interest. Diplomatic influence grows, and the nation negotiates from a position of self-sufficient strength.

units.name: Kobaya
units.text: Fast raiding vessels used by the wokou pirates, light, agile craft built for speed in coastal waters and quick strikes against merchant shipping.

units.name: Yari Ashigaru
units.text: Peasant foot soldiers armed with long yari spears, fighting in disciplined phalanx formations. What they lack in martial training, they compensate with mass and reach.

units.name: Sohei
units.text: Buddhist warrior monks who fight with the fanaticism of the devout. Armed with naginata polearms and hardened by ascetic practice, they are fearsome on the battlefield.

units.name: Ashigaru Teppo
units.text: Massed peasant infantry armed with tanegashima matchlock rifles. What they lack in individual martial skill, they make up in devastating volley fire that can shatter even the finest samurai charge.

units.name: Hayabune
units.text: Fast patrol craft built for speed and maneuverability in the coastal waters of Japan. Ideal for hunting pirates and intercepting smugglers.

units.name: Tekkōsen
units.text: Massive floating fortresses powered by banks of oars and sheathed in iron plate. These ironclads dominate coastal waters with their heavy armament and near-impervious hulls.

units.name: Hatamoto
units.text: The banner-men, direct retainers of the shogun, drawn from the most loyal warrior families. These elite soldiers combine the discipline of professional troops with the martial traditions of the samurai class.

buildings.name: Za Guild Hall
buildings.text: The headquarters of a za merchant guild, where trade monopolies are managed, goods are stored, and fees are collected from members operating under the guild's protection.

buildings.name: Zen Garden
buildings.text: A contemplative garden of raked gravel, carefully placed stones, and meditative spaces attached to a Zen temple complex. A place of artistic refinement and spiritual calm.

buildings.name: Yamashiro
buildings.text: A mountain fortress exploiting Japan's rugged terrain, narrow approaches, steep slopes, and fortified baileys that make assault nearly suicidal for attacking forces.

buildings.name: Jokamachi
buildings.text: A castle town: the administrative and commercial heart of a domain. Beneath the walls of the lord's fortress, merchants, artisans, and samurai retainers create a thriving urban center.

buildings.name: Tamahagane Forge
buildings.text: A traditional tatara furnace where iron sand is smelted into tamahagane: the high-carbon steel from which Japan's legendary blades and armor are forged.

buildings.name: Dejima Trading Post
buildings.text: A controlled foreign trading outpost where Dutch and Chinese merchants may conduct business under strict government supervision. A tiny window to the outside world.

buildings.name: Terakoya
buildings.text: A temple school where Buddhist monks and retired scholars teach reading, writing, and arithmetic to the children of commoners. The foundation of Japan's remarkably high literacy rate.

buildings.name: Daiba Battery
buildings.text: A Western-style coastal artillery emplacement built to defend harbors against foreign warships. Combining imported cannon with traditional fortification expertise.

buildings.name: Gunbatsu Headquarters
buildings.text: The command center of Japan's military establishment, where continental campaigns are planned, armies organized, and the logistics of empire coordinated.

buildings.name: Zaibatsu
buildings.text: An industrial-financial conglomerate combining banking, trade, and manufacturing under a single corporate umbrella. The engine of Japan's modernization and the foundation of its economic power.

list.name: Bakuhan-Taisei
list.text: The constitutional foundation of the Edo state, codified after Sekigahara (1600) and ratified by the 1615 Genna armistice. The bakuhan system divided authority between the central Edo Bakufu (which held foreign affairs, coinage, the Five Kaido, and the Tenryo lands) and roughly 270 daimyo who governed their han with broad fiscal and judicial autonomy in return for oaths of loyalty and the kokudaka rice-yield levy. It was a federation by stratification rather than by treaty.

always.name: Cost of Appease the Elites Action

list.name: Sankin-Kotai
list.text: The alternate-attendance system formalised by Tokugawa Iemitsu in the 1635 revision of the Buke Shohatto. Every daimyo was required to maintain a permanent yashiki residence in Edo, leaving his wife and heir there as de-facto hostages, and to alternate his own residence yearly between Edo and his domain. The processions along the Five Kaido bankrupted the great houses, populated Edo with samurai consumers, and bound the daimyo to the shogun's eye.

list.name: Roju and Wakadoshiyori
list.text: The executive heart of the Edo Bakufu. Four to five Senior Councillors (Roju), drawn from the loyalist fudai daimyo, governed the realm in monthly rotation; the Junior Councillors (Wakadoshiyori) handled the affairs of the shogun's hatamoto bannermen. A rotating Tairo (Great Elder) was appointed in crises. The councillor system replaced the personal rule of the early shoguns with a collegial bureaucracy of chamberlains by the late seventeenth century.

list.name: Hyojosho
list.text: The supreme court of the Edo Bakufu, convening the three magistracies (the Jisha-bugyo for temples and shrines, the Machi-bugyo for the city of Edo, and the Kanjo-bugyo for the treasury) under the chairmanship of a senior Roju. The Hyojosho heard cases that crossed jurisdictional boundaries, appeals from the han, and capital matters affecting the bakufu's interest. Its 1742 codification under the Kujikata Osadamegaki gave the Tokugawa state a unified judicial procedure for the first time.

list.name: Buke Shohatto
list.text: The thirteen-article code regulating the daimyo and their samurai retainers, promulgated by Tokugawa Hidetada in 1615 and revised by Iemitsu in 1635. The articles limited castle construction, marriage alliances, factional contact, and the size of armed retinues; the code was read aloud at the start of every shogun's reign. Buke Shohatto bound the warrior class as a legal estate of the realm and reserved legitimate violence to the shogun alone.

list.name: Sakoku and the Nagasaki Bugyo
list.text: The closed-country regime imposed by Iemitsu's edicts of 1633 to 1639, which sealed Japan from foreign contact except through four narrow channels: the Dutch factory at Dejima, Chinese junks at Nagasaki, Korean embassies through Tsushima, and Ryukyuan tribute through Satsuma. The Nagasaki Bugyo, a magistrate appointed by the bakufu, controlled the Dejima exchange, censored Western books, and received the annual Dutch fusetsugaki intelligence reports. Sakoku preserved domestic stability at the cost of cutting Japan off from the European arms revolution.

list.name: Kuge Shohatto
list.text: The 1615 code regulating the Kyoto Imperial Court that paired with the Buke Shohatto. The kuge nobility centred on the Tenno was confined to scholarship and ritual, and all court business routed through a bakufu-appointed liaison, the Kyoto Shoshidai. The arrangement preserved the emperor's theological legitimacy as the source of the shogun's mandate while stripping the court of any practical authority. The dual residence of legitimacy at Kyoto and authority at Edo defined the Edo state until 1868.

list.name: Dochu Bugyo and the Five Kaido
list.text: The Highway Magistrate's office governing the Five Kaido (Tokaido, Nakasendo, Koshu Kaido, Oshu Kaido, and Nikko Kaido) which radiated from the Nihonbashi bridge in Edo. The 248 post-stations along these roads provided horses, porters, and lodging to officials, daimyo gyoretsu, and licensed travellers. The road network underpinned sankin-kotai, carried the bakufu's couriers and tax-rice, and enabled the mass civilian travel that produced the floating-world culture of Hokusai and Hiroshige.
